name: Obsidian note-taking and knowledge organization patterns
summary:
**Conversation overview**

The user requested research on how people actually use Obsidian for general knowledge work, specifically focusing on research workflows, thought capture, and knowledge base building rather than niche hobby applications. Claude conducted comprehensive research across Reddit, Obsidian forums, and personal blogs, synthesizing real user experiences into a detailed report covering academic research pipelines, daily note workflows, mobile capture solutions, Zettelkasten implementations, and organizational strategies. The research revealed a universal pattern where users initially over-engineer their systems with complex plugins and methodologies, then simplify to focus on actual writing and linking. Key findings included the dominance of Zotero for academic workflows, the centrality of daily notes as organizational anchors, persistent mobile capture friction leading to creative workarounds, and the practical convergence on using folders for workflow status, links for topic relationships, tags for classification, and properties for queryable data.

The user then revealed their specific pain point: generating many small, unrelated thoughts daily that they capture in daily notes but struggle to properly organize by day's end. Claude explained that this is the most common friction point in the Obsidian community and that experienced users typically abandon the end-of-day sorting ritual entirely. Instead of trying to categorize every thought, successful approaches include treating daily notes as permanent homes for most thoughts, using search for retrieval, and only promoting thoughts to dedicated notes when they naturally accumulate enough substance to warrant expansion. When the user asked for clarification about linked notes, Claude explained Obsidian's core linking mechanism using double brackets to create bidirectional connections between notes, which forms the foundation of the tool's knowledge management capabilities.

input.command:
Research how people are using Obsidian (the note-taking app) for general knowledge work, note-taking, and organizing their thoughts. Focus on real user experiences shared in forums, Reddit (r/ObsidianMD, r/PKMS, r/Zettelkasten, etc.), blog posts, and community discussions. 

The focus should be on:
1. **Research workflows** — How people use Obsidian to do research (academic, professional, personal). How they organize research notes, link ideas, use tags vs folders vs links, manage references, etc.
2. **Thought capture and journaling** — How people use Obsidian to note down thoughts, fleeting ideas, reflections. Daily notes workflows, inbox systems, progressive summarization, etc.
3. **Knowledge base building** — How people build a personal knowledge base or "second brain" in Obsidian. Zettelkasten methods, MOCs (Maps of Content), atomic notes, evergreen notes, etc.
4. **Organizational philosophies and structures** — What folder structures, tagging systems, linking strategies, and naming conventions people use. PARA method, Johnny Decimal, flat structures vs deep hierarchies, etc. How their organizational approach relates to what kind of content they're capturing.
5. **Evolution of workflows** — How people's systems have changed over time. What they started with vs what they settled on. Common mistakes and lessons learned.

EXCLUDE very niche/hobby-specific use cases like tracking movies/TV shows, D&D campaign management, recipe collections, etc. These are straightforward database-like uses tied to specific plugins. Focus on the more general, intellectual use cases.

Search across Reddit, Obsidian community forums, blog posts, YouTube creator discussions, and any other relevant sources where real users share their workflows. Prioritize authentic user experiences over marketing content or generic "how to use Obsidian" tutorials.

content.text: Your Obsidian workflow research report is ready. It synthesizes real user practices from Reddit, community forums, and personal blogs—covering academic research pipelines, daily note workflows, mobile capture workarounds, Zettelkasten implementations, and organizational strategies using folders, tags, and links. The report documents the universal over-engineering-to-simplification arc and highlights what experienced users with thousands of notes actually keep in their systems long-term.

input.title: How Obsidian Users Actually Build Their Second Brains: Workflows, Simplification, and What Survives
input.content:
# How Obsidian users actually build their second brains

The single most consistent finding across hundreds of real user accounts is that **nearly everyone over-engineers their Obsidian system first, then simplifies it**. The tools, plugins, and methodologies that dominate YouTube tutorials and setup showcases are frequently the same ones users later abandon. What survives the simplification arc is remarkably consistent: daily notes as a backbone, links over folders for topic organization, search-first navigation, and a philosophical shift from "organizing notes" to "actually writing." This report synthesizes authentic workflows from Reddit, Obsidian community forums, and personal blogs — from PhD researchers with 8,000+ notes to journalists, physicians, and software developers — to map how real people use Obsidian for knowledge work.

## The research vault: from Zotero pipeline to personal Wikipedia

Academic researchers represent Obsidian's most methodical users, and their workflows reveal a surprisingly standardized pipeline. **Zotero dominates as the reference manager** across nearly every academic workflow documented. The typical flow runs: read and annotate a paper in Zotero → import annotations to Obsidian via the Zotero Integration plugin → process highlights into permanent notes → link concepts across sources. Alexandra Phelan, a law and science academic whose workflow became one of the community's most referenced, names her literature notes using the `@citekey` convention so "the difference between a citation and an internal link to the Literature Note is simply a matter of square brackets." She uses color-coded highlights — yellow for interesting points, blue for thesis, red for critique, green for references to follow up — a system independently adopted by many researchers.

The sharpest divide among research users is whether to keep **one comprehensive note per source or break papers into atomic concept notes**. AI researcher Emile van Krieken, who has catalogued **2,100 papers across 900 hierarchical topics** in a completely flat vault (zero folders), explicitly rejects popular PKM methodologies as "too bloated, rigid, or abstract." He organizes entirely through typed links and note-type tags like `#source/paper`, `#topic`, and `#concept`, calling aliases "probably the most underused but powerful feature in core Obsidian." A PhD musicologist known as "Girl in Blue Music" takes the opposite approach, breaking every paper into atomic notes and reassembling them on Obsidian's Canvas — replacing the physical notecard method she previously used by lining index cards on her floor. She frames it as "making my own Wikipedia of everything I've read and learned, organized by idea instead of source."

Medieval historian ryan1992reading offers a candid admission that resonates across the community: the friction of creating a separate note for every idea tempts users to "lump various ideas together simply because I don't feel I've got enough time or energy to separate them out properly." His hard-learned lesson was that **atomic notes should have been combined into outline or structure notes much earlier** — "a classic case of the collecting, rather than thinking, mentality." Professional users like journalist MitchWagner bypass this tension entirely, using one folder per project with an index note linking to everything inside it: "project folders have worked for me for a long time, and I should just stick with that system."

Inger Mewburn, the academic behind Thesis Whisperer who has produced seven books in eight years, anchors her system on a different principle: "the original information is always re-findable on the web, but the notes and highlights I make are irreplaceable." She routes Kindle highlights through Readwise into Obsidian automatically, describing the first sync as importing "hundreds of highlights from nearly 200 academic books." Her reference manager journey — Endnote, Papers, Mendeley, finally Zotero — mirrors the tool-hopping arc that precedes most settled systems.

## Capturing thoughts: daily notes, inboxes, and the friction problem

Daily notes serve as the gravitational center of most Obsidian workflows, but how people use them varies dramatically. Dann Berg, who migrated from Roam Research, structures his daily note around four morning reflection questions, ephemeral bullet-point entries throughout the day, and auto-generated Dataview lists of notes created and modified that day. "Writing in bullet points makes the task much less daunting," he explains. "You're inviting yourself to make a quick note." Product designer Charlie Chao runs his daily note as a digital Bullet Journal, triggered each morning by an iOS automation tied to his wake-up alarm. His entries mix tasks, meal logs, runs with distance and pace, and "TIL" learning notes — all navigable via emoji signifiers like 🧠 for learning and 💭 for reflection. The recall payoff is concrete: "I was eating at a ramen restaurant with my family and wanted to remember what I had there a year ago. So I opened Obsidian on my phone and searched for the restaurant's name."

**Mobile capture remains the community's most persistent pain point.** Obsidian's mobile app requires loading the full vault, which for users with thousands of notes means several seconds of delay — enough to lose a fleeting thought. This has spawned an ecosystem of workarounds: Maggie Delano built a complete inbox-processing system using iOS Shortcuts and Keyboard Maestro macros that create timestamped notes via Obsidian's Advanced URI plugin, then automated three processing commands (Archive, Trash, Move) each bound to a single hotkey. John Mavrick created an entire separate app, Fleeting Notes, specifically for lightweight mobile capture that syncs back to Obsidian. Others use Apple Watch Siri shortcuts, Android quick-capture widgets, or the Drafts app as a staging area.

The journaling community splits into two philosophical camps. Structured-prompt users like Mike Schmitz adopt Marshall Goldsmith's "Daily Questions" method — intention-based questions scored 1-10 ("Did I do my best to ___?"), tracked over time via the Tracker plugin and reviewed quarterly. Free-form users like forum member beadwood found prompts made journaling feel "mechanical" and switched to narrative brain dumps, then used GPT-3 via the Text Generator plugin to auto-tag entries with tone ratings from -5 to +5 — preserving the freedom of freeform writing while adding searchable structure after the fact. Forum user writtenfool abandoned prompts entirely in favor of organic linking: "I highlight 'e-bike' and surround it with `[[e-bike]]` to make it a link. At some point, I'll get self-prompted to see what I've written about my e-bike life."

Christian Houmann, creator of the QuickAdd plugin, runs perhaps the most sophisticated review system documented in the community: daily entries timestamped throughout the day (`- 09:34 Daily QT.`), fields for weight, sleep, energy, and day rating in frontmatter, and a weekly review template that **auto-aggregates all daily data via Dataview** — including wins tagged with `#wins`, areas for improvement tagged `#improve`, and project mentions pulled from daily notes. His key design principle: "It's not a chore. I don't have to write my daily notes. Skipping a day doesn't break anything. And it shouldn't."

## Building a knowledge base: what Zettelkasten actually looks like in practice

The gap between Zettelkasten theory and practice is one of the Obsidian community's most discussed tensions. Bob Doto, author of *A System for Writing*, provides a corrective that reframes the entire conversation: "A zettelkasten is first and foremost a writing tool meant to create an external notes environment riddled with trains of thought that can be pulled from and expanded on in written content. **If your objective isn't to become a publishing machine, then there's no real need for atomic notes or the zettelkasten.**"

In practice, users who successfully maintain Zettelkasten-style systems share several traits. Tim Miller of Obsidian Rocks, with **4,500+ notes**, describes his permanent note rules: one "big idea" per note, understandable without context, written in your own words, linked to other notes. His early attempts failed because his notes "relied heavily on context, and when I forgot the context, the note became useless." Maps of Content became his primary organizational tool — when a MOC accumulates more than six unorganized notes, he sorts them into logical groupings with headers, using Dataview queries to surface unsorted links automatically. Christian Houmann describes seeing **"compound interest" in his knowledge vault** after separating book highlights into atomic notes: "The total value of my knowledge vault increased exponentially with each new note because it could be linked to existing notes."

But not everyone finds atomic notes workable. Forum user Dat, in one of the community's most substantive critiques, describes creating "hundreds of notes in an increasingly specific manner, to the point where there was little text involved apart from the 2-line-long titles." His alternative: use a character-count limit instead of chasing an "ill-defined element like an atomic concept," allowing notes to grow and split naturally through what he calls "mitosis." Forum user Dor adds historical nuance: atomic notes and Zettelkasten "are more suitable for those who write the courses, and even more suitable for those doing the fundamental research" — not for students processing pre-structured teaching.

The **graph view, Obsidian's most visually distinctive feature, is widely regarded as practically limited at scale**. A PhD researcher with 8,000+ notes and 4.5 years of experience reports: "I honestly struggle to find those so-called unexpected connections within such a complex structure. In my daily usage, I often discover unexpected links through keyword searches, Linked Mentions, and tags." The community consensus is that local graph view (connections to the current note) has utility, but the global graph becomes "a mess" beyond roughly 1,000 notes. Real serendipitous discovery happens through search, backlinks, and deliberate review practices — not through staring at a web of nodes.

Steph Ango, CEO of Obsidian, models what a mature, minimal knowledge base looks like. Most of his notes live in the vault root. He navigates via quick switcher, backlinks, or links within notes — rarely the file explorer. His "fractal journaling" creates timestamped thought notes throughout the day, which he reviews every few days, compiles monthly, and reviews yearly — "a fractal web of my life that I can zoom in and out of at varying degrees of detail." His "random revisit" practice, where he periodically uses the random note hotkey to travel through his vault, is deliberately manual: "People have asked me if this could be automated with language models but I do not care to do so. I enjoy this process. Doing this maintenance helps me understand my own patterns. **Don't delegate understanding.**"

## The great organizational debate: folders, tags, links, and the systems people actually keep

Obsidian's flexibility means every user must answer the "where do I put this?" question — and the community has produced years of passionate, contradictory advice. The landscape resolves into a few clear patterns.

**Folder philosophies** span a full spectrum. Steph Ango uses five functional folders (Root, References, Clippings, Attachments, Daily, Templates) with most notes in root. Tim Miller developed FINVA — five folders organized by workflow status rather than topic: Fleeting, In Progress, Notes, Views (MOCs), Archives. The physician at ExcellentPhysician.com uses numbered type-based folders (`01 Notes`, `02 Journal`, `03 Meetings`, `04 References`, `05 Creations`). Stephen Millard spent 3-4 months sketching Johnny Decimal approaches before committing to a reorganization of thousands of notes. Brandon Boswell argues PARA "is not flat enough" for Obsidian because "a file can only be in one folder" while "the structure of your files emerges through the references and use of that note via your graph database." Tim Miller tried PARA for years: "I never really understood the difference between 'projects' and 'areas,' even 'resources' was too nebulous for me."

The tags-versus-links-versus-folders debate has produced a practical consensus among experienced users, even as beginners endlessly relitigate it. A highly-upvoted forum guide by realactualprice identifies the key functional differences: **links auto-refactor when you rename files while tags do not**; tags are implicit counters; tags support hierarchy (`#level1/level2`); links can have aliases; clicking a tag opens search while clicking a link opens a note. Forum user ryadaj uses Library of Congress Subject Headings as a controlled vocabulary for tags, arguing that "tag searches are my primary mode of discovery." Physicist motz manages about 1,000 academic papers with tags like `#Finite_size_effects` and `#Spin_Glass`, noting that "the consistency question of `#dog` vs `#dogs` is not a problem when you have auto-complete."

The most practical organizational wisdom comes from harr, a forum user with **10,000+ notes and 4+ years of experience**, whose lessons earned the most community engagement:

- "I use less plugins and simpler plugins. I find it much easier to organize large vaults *without* Templater and *without* Dataview."
- "I use every organizing tool that plain Obsidian has to offer: links *and* tags *and* properties *and* folders. I combine them in many variations. I don't listen to YouTubers who preach that you should *not* do something."
- "I embrace messiness. I don't strive for 'the perfect system' anymore."
- "Unique filenames and Quick Switcher go a loooooong way."
- "A vault with less than 100 notes doesn't need any particular 'system'."

## The simplification arc: what every experienced user learns the hard way

The most striking pattern across all sources is the universality of the over-engineering-to-simplification trajectory. Tech writer Parth Shah describes it with painful clarity: "I fell into the same trap as everyone else: I spent more time watching 'perfect workflow' videos and installing aesthetic plugins than actually writing." He went from 20+ plugins to bare essentials, realizing his Dataview dashboards — like the automated "books I might read someday" tracker — never once prompted him to actually read a chapter. His graph view obsession led him to create "artificial connections that didn't actually mean anything to my research" just to achieve the "Galaxy Brain" aesthetic he could "show off on Reddit."

Software developer Eric Binnion's documented journey maps the typical timeline: daily notes only (Phase 1), PARA attempt that "never really clicked" (Phase 2), then a simplified numbered-folder structure where 90% of daily use happens in daily notes (Phase 3). His advice: "simply begin. Don't worry too much about having the best workflow or structure." Forum user I-d-as represents the cautionary extreme — tried atomizing notes, properties, tags, MOCs, voice recordings, Excalidraw, complex Dataview queries, and ended up with "a vault that doesn't even know itself." The rescue approach from forum user Pixionus: create a `2.0` folder for new clean notes alongside the old mess, using a plant maturity system (🌱 Seedling → 🌿 Budding → 🌲 Evergreen) that "gamifies it enough that I enjoy 'weeding' from time to time."

**The "aha moment" typically arrives 3-6 months in**, and it is almost always triggered by removing something — a plugin, a folder structure, an expectation — rather than adding it. Nicholas Seitz invokes Gall's Law: "Every functional complex system emerges out of a simpler system that worked first. You have to earn complexity." Matt Giaro, who runs a six-figure writing business from 3,000+ Obsidian notes, puts it bluntly: "Always remember that we want to work IN the system, not ON the system. Luhmann's original Zettelkasten worked because it was easy to maintain. Not because it was complicated."

The Dataview plugin crystallizes this tension. Forum user sprout dropped it entirely after realizing that "the task of actually linking notes has become something I *actually* do, and I have found that doing a couple of things manually has improved my thinking and relating abilities." Counter-perspective from forum user myhatma: "Obsidian without Dataview is like driving your Lambo to the nearest grocery store and back." The truth likely depends on vault purpose — Dataview excels for structured academic literature tracking (Alexandra Phelan's dynamic reading-status tables) but can become an elaborate distraction for personal knowledge work.

## Conclusion: the system that works is the one you actually use

Three insights emerge that the Obsidian community rarely states explicitly. First, **organizational methodology matters far less than the habit of writing in your own words**. Every productive user interviewed — from the AI researcher with 2,100 papers to the journalist with decades of experience — converges on this point. Emile van Krieken: "Do not use LLMs to write your notes. The whole point of taking notes (and learning!) is to write them in your own words." The notes that persist and compound in value are the ones that required genuine cognitive effort to create.

Second, the real differentiator between abandoned vaults and thriving ones is not the organizational system but **the presence of a review practice**. Users who process their inbox, revisit old notes, compile periodic reviews, or do Steph Ango's "random revisit" ritual consistently report that their systems deliver compounding returns. Users without a review practice accumulate notes that sit inert, no matter how cleverly organized.

Third, the community has quietly converged on a structural pattern that rarely appears in tutorials: **folders for workflow status, links for topic relationships, tags for classification metadata, and properties for machine-queryable attributes**. This "use everything for what it's good at" approach, articulated most clearly by the 10K-note veteran harr, resolves the tags-vs-folders-vs-links debate not by picking a winner but by recognizing that each tool solves a different problem. The users who struggle most are those trying to force one tool to do everything — whether that's folders for topics, tags for navigation, or links for status tracking. The users who thrive embrace what Steph Ango calls "chaos and laziness" — minimal upfront structure, heavy linking, and trust that search and connections will surface what matters when it matters.

summaries.summary: Thinking about organizing scattered daily thoughts into structured categories.
Synthesizing research on thought organization systems.
Synthesized common organizational challenges and curated practical solutions.

content.text:
This is probably the single most common friction point people report — and it's worth saying upfront that the research strongly suggests **you might be putting too much pressure on yourself to "correctly place" every thought**. Many experienced users eventually realized that most fleeting thoughts don't need a permanent home at all.

Here's how I'd break down the approaches people have found workable for this exact problem:

**The inbox-triage model.** Several users treat their daily note (or a dedicated "Inbox" note) as a zero-commitment dumping ground, then process it with a ruthless filter. The key insight from users like Dann Berg and Christian Houmann is that processing doesn't mean "find the right folder for every item." It means asking: *does this thought actually deserve to become its own note, or is it fine right here?* Most thoughts — the vast majority — are fine staying as a bullet point in the daily note, forever. They did their job by being written down. You can find them later with search if you ever need them.

**The "don't process at all" approach.** This is closer to what Steph Ango (Obsidian's CEO) does. He writes timestamped thoughts into daily notes throughout the day and reviews them every few days — not to sort them into the "right place," but to notice if any thought has enough gravity to deserve expansion. The ones that do get turned into their own note and linked. The ones that don't just stay in the daily note. The daily note *is* the correct place. His point is that search is powerful enough that you don't need to pre-organize for retrieval.

**The "let it grow" pattern.** This might be the most relevant for you. Instead of trying to classify each thought at the end of the day, you just tag or loosely link them inline as you write — like `[[focus]]` or `#creativity` — and then move on. Over days and weeks, if you keep writing about a topic, you'll notice (through backlinks or search) that it has accumulated enough material to deserve its own note. At that point, pulling the relevant bits together feels natural rather than forced, because you actually have something to say. The note "earns" its existence. Forum user Dat called this "mitosis" — notes split when they're ready, not when you decide they should.

**The practical shift that helps most people.** The struggle you're describing often comes from an implicit assumption that every thought belongs to a topic, and every topic needs a location. But thoughts don't always map to topics — sometimes they're reactions, half-formed questions, or observations that connect to three things at once. Trying to file them forces a false categorization. The users with the most sustainable systems tend to accept that **the daily note is the natural home for unstructured thoughts**, and only promote a thought to its own note when they find themselves returning to it or building on it. The daily note isn't a temporary staging area — it's a legitimate organizational unit.

If you want a concrete minimal workflow: write everything into your daily note. At the end of the day (or every few days), scan through and ask just one question per item: *do I want to think more about this?* If yes, turn it into a `[[linked note]]` right there in the daily note, and go write a few more sentences in that new note. If no, leave it. That's it. No folders, no tags, no sorting. Over time, the notes that matter will accumulate links and substance, and the ones that don't will remain searchable in their daily notes.

The hard truth from the community: the end-of-day sorting ritual is one of the first things people abandon, and the ones who abandoned it earliest tend to be the happiest with their systems.

content.thinking: The user is asking a basic question about what a linked note is in Obsidian. This is a straightforward concept I can explain without any tools.

summaries.summary: Thinking about defining and explaining linked notes.
Identified straightforward Obsidian concept requiring no external resources.

content.text:
In Obsidian, a linked note is just a note that's referenced from another note using the `[[double bracket]]` syntax. When you type `[[something]]` in any note, Obsidian turns that into a clickable link. If a note called "something" already exists, it opens it. If it doesn't exist yet, clicking the link creates it.

So in the context of what I was describing — say you wrote in your daily note:

> Had a thought about how procrastination might actually be an emotional regulation problem, not a time management one `[[procrastination as emotion regulation]]`

That bracketed text becomes a link. You can click it, it creates a new note with that title, and you can write more about the idea there. Meanwhile, back in your daily note, that line is now connected to the new note. If three weeks later you have another thought about the same thing in a different daily note and link to `[[procrastination as emotion regulation]]` again, both daily notes now point to the same place — and that note's "backlinks" panel will show you every place you've ever referenced it.

That's really the core mechanic of Obsidian. It's what makes it different from just having a folder of text files — notes can reference each other, and those connections are bidirectional and automatic. The graph view everyone talks about is just a visualization of all these `[[links]]` between notes.
